title: LPIC-2 Foundations: Resource Diagnosis & Capacity Evidence
purpose: Eight offline real-Linux lessons: record observations, separate symptoms from causes and make a qualified capacity recommendation. Recommended sequence, no unlocks. Completion is self-reviewed and unscored.
prerequisites: Paths, reading output, the text/report unit and Processes, Jobs & Priorities. Read timed commands before typing; all work is inside the unprivileged guest.
coverage: LPIC-2 v4.5 partial 200.1 resource measurement/interpretation and 200.2 trends/forecasting. No network measurements, sar/iostat/iotop, monitoring-platform configuration or full LPIC-2 coverage. Synthetic datasets are teaching examples, not this VM’s history.

entries.description: Capture a dated baseline before diagnosing a performance problem.
troubleshooting: Missing vmstat is a prerequisite failure; do not install packages or substitute invented output.
If workspace setup failed, stop before redirects and create a new valid workspace.
cleanup: No workload was created. Keep baseline.txt for review. Optional removal: only while PWD equals your recorded work directory, remove baseline.txt; leave it with cd "$HOME" and use rmdir "$work" only when empty. Never use recursive removal.
observations: baseline.txt and sampling interval; CPU count, memory available, byte/inode availability.
questions: What can this snapshot establish? What additional observation would you collect before diagnosing a fault?
limitations: One CPU worker only: timeout sends TERM at 12 seconds, then KILL after 2 seconds if necessary. File-I/O commands have 15-second timers plus 2 seconds. These are practical supervision bounds, not guarantees for suspended guests or uninterruptible kernel waits.

Use only the fresh learner-owned workspace. Maximum teaching scratch payload is 16 MiB plus small notes (under 8 KiB per lesson); require at least 528 MiB available before I/O, preserving a 512 MiB reserve. Do not fill disks/inodes, allocate pressure workloads, drop caches, write devices or terminate unrelated tasks.

entries.description: Observe one short-lived CPU worker without imposing a performance threshold.
troubleshooting: A fast interruption may leave no during.txt/worker.txt; record that and repeat only after jobs is empty.
Status 124 is normal timer expiry; 143 can reflect deliberate TERM. No such process after expiry is not evidence of a leak.
cleanup: if [ -n "$worker" ] && jobs -p | grep -qx "$worker" && [ "$(awk '{print $22}' "/proc/$worker/stat" 2>/dev/null)" = "$birth" ]; then kill -TERM "$worker"; fi; if [ -n "$worker" ]; then wait "$worker" 2>/dev/null || :; fi
Keep the four small observation files. Cleanup never uses pkill, killall or a stale saved PID. On shell loss, let the 12-second timer finish; disk Resume does not recover jobs.
observations: before.txt, during.txt, after.txt, worker.txt; interval, PID/PPID and timeout status.
questions: Did observations support a CPU cause? Could host scheduling or other guest activity explain the difference?

materials:
Guest-local setup (stop if creation or cd fails):
work=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/capacity-cpu.XXXXXX"); cd "$work" && pwd

Approved workload starter (prepare your sampling commands first; no second job):
if [ -z "$(jobs -p)" ]; then timeout -k 2s 12s bash -c 'while :; do :; done' & worker=$!; birth=$(awk '{print $22}' "/proc/$worker/stat"); fi
Track supervisor $worker and actual child using ps. If the timer expires before sampling, retain the inconclusive result; wait/reap before repeating. Cleanup uses the current shell job plus matching start tick, never a stale PID.

entries.description: Observe a small regular-file write/read while preserving a generous space reserve.
troubleshooting: A failed admission guard creates no scratch payload. Do not reduce the reserve to force the exercise.
File too large or timeout is evidence of refusal/failure, not successful throughput. Do not weaken ulimit or rerun larger inputs.
cleanup: I/O runs in the foreground under timeout. Ctrl-C interrupts it; after the prompt returns, remove the exact partial scratch file using the same guard. Keep notes; do not use recursive removal.
observations: Available KiB before/after, file byte count, both timing/error files and whether each command succeeded.
questions: What does conv=fsync request, and what can the guest still not establish about physical durability? Is a rounded zero elapsed value a valid denominator?
limitations: One CPU worker only: timeout sends TERM at 12 seconds, then KILL after 2 seconds if necessary. File-I/O commands have 15-second timers plus 2 seconds. These are practical supervision bounds, not guarantees for suspended guests or uninterruptible kernel waits.

materials:
Guest-local setup (stop if creation or cd fails):
work=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/capacity-io.XXXXXX"); cd "$work" && pwd

Approved guarded scratch write (Bash default ulimit units; stop on failure):
test "$PWD" = "$work" && available=$(df -Pk . | awk 'NR==2 {print $4}') && [ "$available" -ge 540672 ] && TIMEFORMAT='%3R seconds' && { time ( ulimit -f 16384; timeout -k 2s 15s dd if=/dev/zero of=io.bin bs=1M count=16 conv=fsync status=none ); } 2> write-time.txt

Approved bounded scratch read:
test "$PWD" = "$work" && TIMEFORMAT='%3R seconds' && { time timeout -k 2s 15s dd if=io.bin of=/dev/null bs=1M count=16 status=none; } 2> read-time.txt

entries.description: Calculate a reserve-aware forecast and recognize insufficient evidence.
troubleshooting: Do not mix KiB/MiB or forecast against the actual VM disk; 1000/100 are hypothetical policy values.
If sample days coincide, fix the data rather than divide by zero. No positive rate means no finite linear exhaustion estimate.
cleanup: No workload. Keep the three small files; optional cleanup removes only their exact names in your recorded workspace.
observations: Both labeled synthetic tables, forecast.txt, independent arithmetic and uncertainty statement.
questions: When could a correct calculation still be a poor forecast? What would you collect before committing money or a maintenance date?

entries.description: Combine observations and uncertainty into a defensible operational handover.
troubleshooting: nano is in the pinned image; if unavailable report the mismatch, do not install it.
App Next/completion clicks do not validate a report. Placeholder text and a screenshot alone do not establish understanding.

observations: baseline.txt, history.txt, forecast.txt and your edited recommendation.txt.
questions: Which statement is directly observed, calculated, assumed or still unknown? What evidence would change your recommendation?
